The speaker moved the second reading of the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019, arguing it would allow authorities to delay the return of Australians of counterterrorism concern for up to two years and impose conditions on return, citing that around 230 Australians had travelled to Syria or Iraq since 2012 with about 80 still active. The bill includes independent review of ministerial decisions and a return permit process.

The Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2019 was introduced to add accountability and transparency measures to the temporary exclusion order scheme, implementing recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security. It amends the Intelligence Services Act 2001 to give the committee monitoring and review powers, requires a review of the scheme within three years, and allows the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor to review the scheme on their own initiative.

The government has rejected at least 10 bipartisan recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security on the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 without explanation, breaching a long-standing compact on national security legislation. The bill should be amended to conform to the committee's recommendations and referred back for further scrutiny.

The speaker argued in favour of the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 and against the Isaacs amendment, citing 16 disrupted terrorist attacks since 2014, nearly 230 Australian citizens who travelled to Syria and Iraq, and approximately 80 still active in conflict zones, while detailing the bill's provisions for ministerial discretion, judicial review, and child-specific safeguards.

The speaker argued that the government's temporary exclusion orders bill ignores recommendations from its own parliamentary committee and lacks long-term deradicalisation and international coordination strategies, despite $13 million promised for deradicalisation programs and $60 million for counter-terrorism.

The speaker argued for the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019, which would allow the minister to control the return of Australian citizens of counterterrorism interest from overseas conflict zones, citing around 230 Australians who have travelled to Syria or Iraq since 2012.

The speaker argued that the Counter-Terrorism (Temporary Exclusion Orders) Bill 2019 is essential to delay, control and risk-manage the return of foreign fighters, and expressed support for the bill in its present form while opposing Labor's amendments. The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2019-07-30.118.1) introduced by MP for Isaacs [Mark Dreyfus](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/isaacs/mark_dreyfus), which means it failed. Mr Dreyfus [explained his amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2019-07-30.118.1) as: > *a very simple amendment. The effect of it would be to extend the sunset date for the questioning warrant power until 7 December 2019 and to retain the existing sunset date for the questioning and detention warrant power of 7 September 2019. That's the power that's never been used.* ### What does the bill do? This bill was introduced to extend the operation of certain special powers relating to suspected terrorism offences to 7 September 2020. Currently, those powers are due to sunset (that is, stop being part of our law) on 7 September 2019. ### What are the special powers? The special powers extended by this bill are the power to issue questioning warrants (QWs) and questioning and detention warrants (QDWs) in relation to suspected terrorism offences. They are extraordinary because they can be issued in relation to someone even though they are not suspected of, or charged with, any offence. In other words, these warrants are an intelligence-gathering and preventative power. Someone might be subject to these warrants because they can provide information about a potential terrorism offence and they may be detained in order to prevent them from damaging evidence or alerting someone involved in a terrorism offence that their actions are being investigated. These powers have been extended several times since they were first introduced in 2002. More information is available in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1920a/20bd004).

The opposition supported the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019, which provides Efic with an extra $1 billion in callable capital, renames it Export Finance Australia, and introduces an Australian benefits test for loans funding Pacific infrastructure; the bill was referred to a Senate inquiry reporting by 26 March 2019. The speech noted bipartisan backing, citing Bill Shorten's proposed Pacific infrastructure investment bank and the government's $2 billion Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific, and suggested examining the US BUILD Act and UK CDC Group as alternative models.

The bill provides the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation with an additional $1 billion in capital for commercial infrastructure loans in the Pacific, subject to an Australian benefit test. The speaker also criticised the coalition government for neglecting Pacific relations, particularly through climate change inaction and $11 billion in aid cuts.

The speaker argued that Australia should support Pacific infrastructure through the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment Bill 2019, providing an additional $1 billion in callable capital for loans on a commercial basis, to boost regional prosperity, security, and economic integration while also benefiting Australian exporters like those in Tasmania.

The speaker argued that the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment Bill is welcome but overdue, and criticised the government for failing to take the Pacific seriously, citing the Prime Minister's absence from the September Pacific Islands Forum, Environment Minister Melissa Price's reported "chequebook" comment to former Kiribati president Anote Tong, and the agriculture visa debacle, while supporting the Seasonal Worker Program and calling for a credible climate change policy.

The speaker supported the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019, which renames Efic to Export Finance Australia and provides an extra $1 billion in callable capital for infrastructure financing in the Pacific, including East Timor, with a new Australian benefits test replacing the previous one-third Australian content requirement. The speaker noted bipartisan agreement on Pacific funding, referenced the opposition leader’s October 2018 announcement and the Prime Minister’s subsequent similar announcement, and called for Senate committee scrutiny to address concerns about project quality and unintended consequences.

The speaker expressed concerns about the bill's $1 billion increase in callable capital for Efic and the lack of accompanying policy frameworks, noted Labor's prior proposal for a government-backed infrastructure investment bank, and criticised the government for cutting $11 billion in development assistance over five years.

The Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019 received bipartisan support to enhance Australia's infrastructure investment in the Pacific, with Efic to operate under the trading name Export Finance Australia.

The Greens moved an amendment to prohibit the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation (Efic) from funding or facilitating thermal coal mining and export on a commercial scale, including projects like the Adani coalmine, and criticised the government for secretly altering Efic's mandate in 2017 to allow coal funding.

The Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 was introduced to address the erosion of law enforcement and security agencies' investigative capacity due to encryption, creating new industry assistance powers (technical assistance and technical capability notices) without mandating backdoors, expanding computer access warrants, and increasing penalties for failing to assist device access—citing that encryption affected 9 in 10 ASIO priority cases and 200 AFP operations, and encrypted intercepts rose from 3% in June 2013 to over 55% by July 2017.

Labor supported the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 after negotiating amendments to define “systemic weakness,” strengthen oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security and the Commonwealth Ombudsman, and require further review, in order to address risks to national security, US security cooperation, and Australian technology businesses.

The speaker argued that the bill creates a systemic weakness in encrypted communications, threatening privacy, the tech industry, and civil liberties. They opposed rushed passage of the bill and the 50 pages of last-minute amendments, citing past failures like metadata laws that saw 350,000 requests per year, and warned that Australia would become a place where tech developers would avoid working.

Argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 addressed serious terrorism, child abuse, security and privacy issues, but criticised the government's handling and contradictory explanations. Supported targeted assistance powers while opposing systemic weaknesses, back doors and weakened encryption, and backed stronger Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security safeguards.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 risks weakening encryption without adequate judicial oversight, warning that 350,000 metadata requests—including from local councils—demonstrate how security powers can be misused.

The speaker argued the government rushed and politicised the encryption bill, refused judicial oversight for technical assistance and capability notices, and failed to define 'systemic weakness'. Labor reached a compromise to pass the bill before Christmas but maintained concerns.

Opposed the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018, arguing it would build a known vulnerability into encryption software that could be exploited by wrongdoers, and criticised the excessive extension of state power through security reforms including mandatory metadata retention. Also defended the member for Eden-Monaro’s comments and described the member for Hume’s comment as deeply offensive.

The MP criticised the government for rushing the encryption bill without proper consultation, arguing Labor secured amendments to clarify systemic weakness, add oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security and the Ombudsman, and require Attorney-General and communications minister approval for technical capability notices. Labor remains concerned about the lack of judicial oversight for interception-related notices and will monitor the legislation, with the committee inquiry continuing into 2019 and a separate review by the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor within 18 months.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 requires balancing national security with individual privacy, noting that the government rushed the bill through the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security despite bipartisan efforts and 300 amendments on 15 previous national security bills. The speaker criticized Prime Minister Morrison and the Minister for Home Affairs for politicizing the process and ignoring submissions from Australian tech companies, while Labor proposed substantive amendments to address concerns from industry and civil society.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 is urgently needed to help law enforcement and national security agencies access encrypted communications used by criminals and terrorists, citing that 95% of ASIO’s top counterterrorism targets use encryption and referencing recent fatal attacks in Melbourne. The bill introduces new computer access warrants and industry assistance frameworks, prohibits systemic backdoors, and includes safeguards against mass surveillance, with the speaker urging parliamentary support for the bill and agreed amendments.

The speaker criticised the government's handling of the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018, arguing that the process was rushed and interfered with despite a consensus report from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security. They noted the bill is 175 pages, amends 10 acts, and introduces new compulsory powers against innocent third parties, and that the government tabled 173 amendments (covering 50 pages) informally at 6:30 am on the day of debate, with no formal response to the committee's 17 recommendations.
